newsitem.title: USA: U.S. miitary preparing for possible Zaire evacuation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. miitary preparing for possible Zaire evacuation.

text.p: The U.S. military is making contingency preparations for the possible emergency evacuation of Americans from Zaire but has received no request to do so from the embassy in Kinshasa, the Pentagon said on Thursday.

"We have sent in an assessment team and we are taking prudent efforts beyond that to be ready to do whatever we are requested to do," Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters of the continuing civil strife in the central African state.

He refused to go into details about the preparations, but said that he did not believe any U.S. military aircraft or helicopters had been moved into region yet for a possible evacuation of some of the 650 Americans in Zaire.

Bacon said in response to questions that a 30-member U.S. military team sent to Zaire on Wednesday was still assessing the situation in an anti-government rebellion and the possible use of roads, airfields and communications in any emergency movement of Americans.

Zaire remained very unsettled, Bacon said, and the United States was aware of reports of a possible coup attempt against ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is believed to be preparing to return to Kinshasa from Europe on Friday.

"The talk is in the wind and I think we have to pay attention to the fact that there could be rapid change in Kinshasa," he said, while stressing that no request had been made by the American embassy to remove Americans.

There are believed to be about 650 Americans in Zaire, including those working for the American government. France has advised its citizens to leave Zaire and has moved aircraft and about 100 troops to neighbouring Gabon and Congo to be ready for any evacuation of French citizens.

Bacon said that the United States had also advised Americans to leave Zaire, but said that rebels seeking to overthrow the government there were about (625 miles (1,000 km) from Kinshasa and that anyone in danger in the capital could simply cross the Congo River by ferry to reach the adjoining Congo capital of Brazzaville.

Late Thursday, the State Department issued an official warning for U.S. citizens contemplating travel to Zaire and urged all Americans to leave the country due to "the uncertain political and security situation."
"The Department strongly encourages U.S. citizens in Zaire to depart the country," a written statement said. It also urged dependents of U.S. embassy staff to leave Kinshasa.
Spokesman Nicholas Burns said Zaire was discussed at a meeting on Thursday morning chaired by Undersecretary of State Peter Tarnoff but that no decision was taken on evacuation.

Burns also said the United States would contribute to a $240 million U.N. appeal for emergency aid to refugees in the region. "We support this appeal and we will be determining shortly the exact amount of assistance that we will donate," he told reporters.
If the situation in Zaire deteriorates suddenly and Americans are evacuated, it would be the second such move by U.S. troops in a foreign country in recent days.

U.S. Marines began evacuating Americans from Albania's capital of Tirana last weekend and Bacon said that one American and 13 other persons were removed on Thursday. He said a total of 860 persons, 395 of them Americans, had now been removed from that strife-torn European state since the helicopter evacuation began.

The Pentagon spokesman said U.S. military aircraft were now flying over the Adriatic away from possible ground fire in Albania after a shoulder-fired missile was launched at an American AC-130 gunship on Sunday.
The heavily-armed, lumbering warplane did not return fire and was out of range of the missile at the time, Bacon said.
